name: Von Flue Choke
summary: The Von Flue Choke is a no-gi blood choke applied while passing toward an opponent's committed guillotine, driving your shoulder into their exposed carotid while their own trapping arm seals the other side to force the tap.
description: Counter a committed guillotine with the Von Flue Choke from side control. Learn shoulder-pressure mechanics, finishing steps, and defense. Success: 35/50/65%.
overview: Named after UFC veteran Jason Von Flue, who popularized the technique against Alberto Crane in 2006, this counter-choke has become a staple deterrent against the over-committed guillotine in no-gi grappling. It transforms a defensive scenario — an opponent clinging to a guillotine grip from bottom as you pass — into an immediate offensive finish, using shoulder pressure and body weight to compress one carotid artery while the opponent's own wrapping arm compresses the other. The technique is especially valuable because it requires no grip changes and no separate setup: the moment an opponent refuses to release a guillotine while you pass toward their choking arm, the finish is available. Beyond the finish itself, the Von Flue carries an outsized psychological effect — once caught with it, opponents become reluctant to hold deep guillotines from bottom, fundamentally changing how they defend your guard passing. It embodies a core BJJ principle: every offensive grip held too rigidly contains the seeds of its own defeat.

injury_risks.injury: Carotid artery compression leading to unconsciousness
injury_risks.recovery_time: Immediate recovery if released promptly, potential brain damage if held past unconsciousness

injury_risks.injury: Neck strain from resisting the choke

safety_considerations.application_speed: SLOW and progressive - 3-5 seconds minimum to allow partner to recognize the danger and release their guillotine grip
tap_signals: Verbal tap (most important as arms may be trapped)
Physical hand tap on your body or mat
Any distress signal including body going limp
release_protocol: Immediately remove shoulder pressure from neck
Lift your head and upper body away from opponent's neck
Create space by posting your hands and moving your torso back
If partner is unconscious, elevate legs and monitor recovery
training_restrictions: Never apply full pressure in training — use gradual pressure to allow tap
Never hold the choke after partner releases their guillotine grip
Always allow partner's arms to be free enough to tap
Never use competition speed or sudden pressure in drilling
Stop immediately if partner's grip loosens (indicates impending unconsciousness)
Require verbal confirmation that partner understands the danger before practicing

variations_and_setups.description: When passing half guard against an opponent holding a guillotine, you can apply the Von Flue choke before fully passing to side control. The setup is identical, but you must be careful to prevent them from using their half guard to sweep you as you apply pressure.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: When opponent maintains guillotine grip from bottom half guard during your passing attempt, allowing you to finish the pass with a submission threat

variations_and_setups.description: If opponent attempts a standing guillotine and you successfully sprawl, you can apply Von Flue pressure from the standing position by driving your shoulder into their neck while they hold the guillotine. This is less common but highly effective in no-gi scrambles.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: Against standing guillotine attempts where opponent refuses to release grip after you've sprawled and established superior position

variations_and_setups.description: As you apply the Von Flue choke, if the opponent attempts to bridge or create space, you can swing your leg over into mount while maintaining shoulder pressure. This creates an even more dominant finishing position with the same choke mechanism.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: When opponent creates upward movement or bridging that makes the mount transition available while you're applying the choke from side control

attacker.name: Von Flue Choke Attacker
attacker.description: Finish the Von Flue Choke from side control: shoulder-pressure mechanics, grip details, execution steps, and counters for this guillotine-defeating blood choke.
attacker.overview: As the attacker, your job is to recognize when an opponent's guillotine has become a liability and convert it into a finish. The Von Flue is not a separate technique you set up; it is a passing choice you make the instant the opponent refuses to release their guillotine. By passing toward their choking arm and driving your near-side shoulder and jaw into the exposed carotid, you complete a blood choke in which the opponent's own wrapping arm seals the opposite side. Success depends on direction of pass, shoulder placement, forward posture to deny their guillotine finish, and patient, body-weight-driven pressure rather than raw shoulder strength.
key_principles: The opponent's guillotine arm becomes one side of your strangle — you only have to seal the other carotid with your shoulder
Always pass toward the choking arm, never away from it; passing away frees their guillotine and removes the choke
Drive your shoulder and the side of your jaw into the exposed carotid, not into the windpipe — this is a blood choke, not an air choke
Maintain heavy, forward head posture so the opponent cannot elevate their hips and finish their own guillotine
Generate pressure with chest connection and a low, advancing base rather than muscling with the shoulder alone
Walk your feet and hips toward the opponent's head to ratchet pressure deeper without changing any grip
Treat recognition speed as the primary skill — the finish is available only while the opponent stubbornly holds the grip
setup_requirements: Opponent is holding a committed guillotine or front headlock and refusing to release it
You are positioned on the same side as the opponent's choking arm and passing toward it
Chest-to-chest or shoulder-to-neck contact is established on the choking-arm side of the neck
Strong forward posture with a heavy head to prevent being guillotined during the pass
A stable, advancing base on knees or feet to drive body weight forward into the neck

execution_steps.description: Identify that the opponent has a deep guillotine and is refusing to release it as you pass, which is the trigger that makes the Von Flue choke available to you.
execution_steps.timing: The instant the opponent commits to and holds the guillotine

execution_steps.description: Direct your pass to the same side as the opponent's choking arm rather than away from it, so your shoulder lines up with the carotid their arm is not covering.
execution_steps.timing: As you begin clearing the legs or hips

execution_steps.action: Drop the shoulder onto the carotid
execution_steps.description: Lower your near-side shoulder and the edge of your jaw onto the exposed side of the opponent's neck, sealing the carotid that their own arm leaves open.

execution_steps.action: Establish chest pressure and a low base
execution_steps.description: Flatten your chest against the opponent and widen your base, transferring body weight through your shoulder into the neck instead of pushing with the arm.
execution_steps.timing: As the shoulder seats on the neck

execution_steps.description: Keep your head heavy and posture forward with your hips back so the opponent cannot elevate their hips to finish their own guillotine while you settle the choke.

execution_steps.action: Walk the hips to ratchet pressure
execution_steps.description: Step your feet and walk your hips toward the opponent's head to drive your shoulder progressively deeper into the carotid, increasing pressure without changing grips.
execution_steps.timing: Once the shoulder line is established

execution_steps.action: Apply progressively and watch for the tap
execution_steps.description: Increase pressure smoothly over several seconds, watching for the verbal or physical tap and releasing instantly, since the opponent's trapped arms may make a hand tap impossible.
execution_steps.timing: Final phase, always with safety priority

common_counters.counter: Opponent releases the guillotine grip immediately
common_counters.your_response: Accept the freed grip and complete your pass to side control top, where you retain dominant position even though the choke is gone.

common_counters.counter: Opponent turns away and tucks the chin to relieve carotid pressure
common_counters.your_response: Follow their turn with your shoulder, keep chest pressure, and continue to side control if the carotid clears.

common_counters.counter: Opponent elevates their hips and finishes their own guillotine before you settle
common_counters.your_response: Re-establish forward posture and a heavy head earlier next time; if caught, defend the guillotine and recover.

common_counters.counter: Opponent frames on your shoulder to keep the carotid line open
common_counters.your_response: Walk your hips toward their head to slip past the frame and re-seat the shoulder on the neck.

common_errors.error: Passing away from the choking arm instead of toward it
common_errors.consequence: You free the opponent's guillotine entirely and the choke disappears, often leaving you in their guillotine instead
common_errors.correction: Always commit your pass to the same side as the opponent's choking arm so your shoulder seals the open carotid

common_errors.error: Pushing with shoulder muscle instead of body weight
common_errors.consequence: The pressure is weak and easily resisted, the choke stalls, and you fatigue your shoulder
common_errors.correction: Connect chest-to-chest and drive weight through a low, advancing base so gravity supplies the pressure

common_errors.error: Posturing up or lifting the head during the finish
common_errors.consequence: You give the opponent room to elevate their hips and finish their own guillotine on you
common_errors.correction: Keep a heavy, forward head and hips back to deny the guillotine while you settle the shoulder

common_errors.error: Rushing the pressure with no tap window
common_errors.consequence: The partner's arms are often trapped and cannot tap in time, creating a high risk of injury or rapid unconsciousness
common_errors.correction: Apply slowly over several seconds and accept verbal or foot taps, releasing the instant any signal appears

common_errors.error: Failing to control the far side, letting the opponent turn out
common_errors.consequence: The opponent rotates their neck and chin away, clearing the carotid and escaping to recover position
common_errors.correction: Maintain chest connection and follow their rotation with your shoulder to keep the carotid sealed

common_errors.error: Misidentifying which arm is the choking arm
common_errors.consequence: You place your shoulder on the wrong side and compress nothing, wasting the opportunity
common_errors.correction: Trace the arm wrapped under the chin and target the carotid on that same side

training_progressions.description: Drill spotting a committed guillotine and instantly calling out the choking-arm side and the correct passing direction, without applying pressure.
Slowly pass toward the choking arm and seat the shoulder on the carotid with a heavy head, holding the position without finishing to ingrain mechanics.
Apply gradual body-weight pressure with a cooperative partner who taps early, building feel for the carotid line and the release timing.
Spar from a guillotine-defense start where the bottom player holds the grip, finishing the Von Flue against progressive resistance while respecting tap signals.

flashcards.question: Which anatomical structures does the Von Flue Choke compress to force the tap?
flashcards.answer: It is a blood choke targeting the carotid arteries: your shoulder and jaw seal one carotid while the opponent's own choking arm compresses the other, cutting blood flow to the brain rather than restricting the airway.

flashcards.question: Your opponent has a tight guillotine and you need to pass — which direction do you pass to set up the Von Flue?
flashcards.answer: You pass toward the choking arm, not away from it, dropping your near-side shoulder onto the exposed carotid so their wrapping arm completes the strangle. Passing away frees their guillotine and removes the choke entirely.

flashcards.question: What must be established before driving shoulder pressure to finish the Von Flue?
flashcards.answer: You need chest-to-chest connection on the choking-arm side, your shoulder and jaw seated on the carotid, a heavy forward head posture to deny their guillotine, and a low advancing base so body weight supplies the pressure.

flashcards.question: As you settle the shoulder, the opponent tries to elevate their hips to finish their guillotine — what prevents them?
flashcards.answer: Maintaining a heavy, forward head with your hips back keeps your posture ahead of their elevation, denying the angle they need to finish the guillotine while your shoulder continues sealing their carotid.

flashcards.question: What signs tell you the Von Flue is cutting blood flow effectively?
flashcards.answer: You feel your shoulder bone seated firmly on the side of the neck, the opponent's guillotine grip begins to weaken, and they reach for a verbal or physical tap; flushing of the face also signals the carotid is being compressed.

flashcards.question: The pressure feels close but not quite enough to finish — what adjustment increases it without losing position?
flashcards.answer: Walk your feet and hips toward the opponent's head to drive your shoulder progressively deeper into the carotid. The Von Flue requires no grip change, so ratcheting with your base is the safest way to add pressure.

flashcards.question: What is the most common error that turns a Von Flue attempt into getting guillotined yourself?
flashcards.answer: Posturing up and lifting your head, or passing away from the choking arm, both free the opponent's guillotine and let them elevate their hips to finish on you. Keep a heavy head and pass toward the choking arm.

flashcards.question: Why must the Von Flue Choke be applied slowly in training, and when do you release?
flashcards.answer: It is a fast-acting blood choke and the partner's arms are often trapped, so they may not be able to hand-tap. Apply over several seconds, accept verbal or foot taps, and release instantly the moment they tap, release their grip, or go limp.

flashcards.question: In a no-gi match an opponent jumps a guillotine from bottom and refuses to let go — how do you turn that defense into a finish?
flashcards.answer: Recognize the Von Flue is available, pass toward the choking arm, drop your shoulder onto the exposed carotid, establish chest pressure with a heavy head, and walk your hips in to finish. The threat also deters future deep guillotines.

flashcards.question: How do you identify the choking arm that completes the Von Flue strangle?
flashcards.answer: Trace the opponent's arm that wraps under their own chin and around your neck; that is the choking arm. You then seat your shoulder on the carotid on that same side, letting their arm seal the opposite carotid.

defender.name: Von Flue Choke Defender
defender.description: Defend the Von Flue Choke: recognize the shoulder-pressure danger of a committed guillotine, release in time, and escape before the carotid is sealed.
defender.overview: As the defender, you are typically the bottom player who threw a guillotine and is now passing into danger. The Von Flue punishes a guillotine held too long while the opponent passes toward your choking arm. Your defense is built on early recognition: the same grip that threatens your opponent becomes the seal on one of your own carotids the instant their shoulder lands on the other side. The highest-percentage answer is almost always to release the guillotine before the carotid is sealed and recover position, rather than stubbornly clinging to a grip that is now choking you. Secondary options involve framing, turning your chin into the choking arm to preserve a blood path, or finishing your guillotine first if it is already deep and high.
key_principles: Your own guillotine arm becomes one side of the choke — holding it too long against a passing opponent is what creates the danger
Release early: a surrendered guillotine and a lost position always beat going unconscious
Recognize the shoulder-pressure cue before the carotid is fully sealed, while you still have time to react
Turn your chin toward the choking arm to keep a blood path open if you cannot release instantly
Never posture flat and leave the carotid exposed under the descending shoulder
Frame and angle away from the pressure rather than bridging straight into the shoulder
Treat a deep, high guillotine as a possible race — finish it first or abandon it, but do not stall in between
recognition_cues: The passing opponent drives a shoulder and the edge of their jaw into the side of your neck where your own arm wraps
Rising, deep pressure on one carotid combined with a sudden feeling of light-headedness
Your opponent is passing toward your choking arm and flattening their chest onto you rather than pulling away
Your guillotine grip suddenly feels like it is helping their pressure instead of threatening them

defensive_options.action: Release the guillotine grip the instant you feel shoulder pressure on your neck
defensive_options.when_to_use: As soon as the top player turns toward your choking arm and drops their shoulder onto the carotid
defensive_options.if_successful: You survive the choke but concede the guard pass and end up in side control bottom
defensive_options.risk: You lose your offensive guillotine threat and a dominant top player consolidates position

defensive_options.action: Frame on the attacker's shoulder and turn your chin into the choking arm to keep a blood path open
defensive_options.when_to_use: When the shoulder is settling but the carotid is not yet fully sealed
defensive_options.if_successful: You preserve blood flow, keep your guillotine alive, and re-threaten the front headlock
defensive_options.risk: Delaying too long allows the carotid to seal and the choke to finish

defensive_options.action: Elevate your hips and finish your own guillotine before the Von Flue seals
defensive_options.when_to_use: When your guillotine is already deep, high, and close to finishing
defensive_options.if_successful: You finish the guillotine or force the top player to abandon the Von Flue and defend
defensive_options.risk: Committing fully can accelerate the Von Flue if your choke is not actually tight

escape_paths: Release the guillotine and hip escape to recover guard before the pass is completed
Turn in toward the attacker and come up to a front headlock or scramble
Bridge and turn to turtle to relieve neck pressure once the grip is released

favorable_outcomes.how: Recognize the Von Flue early, turn your chin toward the choking arm to keep a blood path open, and re-establish a tight guillotine or front-headlock threat that forces the top player to abandon the choke and defend instead of passing.
Release the guillotine the moment the shoulder lands, surrendering the pass to avoid the choke; you end up defending side control bottom but stay conscious and in the match.

common_errors.error: Refusing to release the guillotine as the shoulder pressure builds
common_errors.consequence: The Von Flue seals your carotid and you go unconscious while still clinging to a grip that is choking you
common_errors.correction: Release early — a lost guillotine and a conceded pass are always better than a lost match by submission

common_errors.error: Posturing flat and leaving the carotid exposed
common_errors.consequence: The descending shoulder seals the open carotid instantly with no room for you to react
common_errors.correction: Turn your chin toward the choking arm and frame on the shoulder to keep a blood path open

common_errors.error: Panicking and bridging straight into the shoulder
common_errors.consequence: Bridging into the pressure drives your own neck harder into their shoulder and accelerates the choke
common_errors.correction: Frame and angle away from the pressure, using a hip escape rather than bridging into the shoulder

flashcards.question: What sensation warns you that your guillotine is exposing you to a Von Flue Choke?
flashcards.answer: You feel the passing opponent drive their shoulder and jaw into the side of your neck where your own arm wraps, with rising pressure on that carotid and sudden light-headedness — a sign your guillotine has become the seal on your own choke.

flashcards.question: Your guillotine is deep but the top player drops their shoulder onto your neck — what is the highest-percentage defense?
flashcards.answer: Release the guillotine immediately and turn in to recover guard or scramble before the carotid is sealed. A surrendered grip and a conceded pass are far better than going unconscious clinging to the choke.

flashcards.question: Why is holding a guillotine to the death from bottom dangerous against a passing opponent?
flashcards.answer: Holding it exposes you to the Von Flue: your own wrapping arm becomes one side of a blood choke, so when the opponent seats a shoulder on the other carotid, your grip helps finish the strangle on yourself.

flashcards.question: If you feel light-headed while defending a Von Flue and your arms are trapped, how should you signal?
flashcards.answer: Tap verbally or with your foot or leg immediately — do not wait for a hand tap, since your arms are often trapped in the guillotine. Early tapping prevents unconsciousness and brain injury from carotid compression.

flashcards.question: After releasing your guillotine to avoid the Von Flue, what should you prioritize?
flashcards.answer: Prioritize protecting your neck and immediately framing and hip-escaping to recover guard or turning to turtle. Conceding the pass is acceptable; the goal is to escape the choke and re-establish a defensive structure.

training_progressions.description: Drill from a guillotine where a cooperative partner passes toward the choking arm, practicing identifying the shoulder-pressure cue before any real pressure is applied.
Practice releasing the guillotine and recovering guard or turtle the instant the shoulder lands, building the reflex to choose position over a doomed grip.
Spar from a guillotine-defense start against a top player hunting the Von Flue, choosing in real time whether to finish, frame, or release while respecting tap signals.
